68: I no longer remember where I broke off in my account.
I only know it was two in the morning when I went to bed; and if you had been here, so that I could talk instead of write, I would probably have kept you up till daylight.
69: I do not think I have told you yet what happened as we rode home from the ball, and I have no time to tell you now.
The whole country was fresh, and the rain fell drop by drop from the trees in the forest.
Charlotte asked whether I did not want to sleep as well, and begged me not to stand on ceremony for her sake.
Looking steadily at her, I answered, "As long as I can see those eyes open, there is no danger of my falling asleep."
We both stayed awake until we reached her door.
The maid opened it softly and assured her, in answer to her questions, that her father and the children were well and still sleeping.
I left her, asking leave to visit her later in the day.
She agreed, and I went; and since then the sun and moon and stars may go their own way.
I do not know whether it is day or night; the whole world is nothing to me.
71: My days are as happy as those God keeps for his elect.
And whatever my fate may be hereafter, I can never say that I have not tasted joy — the purest joy of life.
I am now completely settled there.
From that spot I am only half a league from Charlotte; and there I enjoy myself, and taste every pleasure that can fall to a man's lot.
72: Little did I imagine, when I chose Walheim for my walks, that all heaven lay so close to it.
How often, wandering from the hillside or across the meadows by the river, have I looked at this hunting-lodge, which now holds all the joy of my heart!
73: I have often reflected, my dear Wilhelm, on the eagerness men feel to wander and make new discoveries.
And on the secret impulse that afterwards draws them back to their narrow circle, to conform to custom, and to trouble themselves no further with what goes on around them.
74: It is strange how, when I first came here and looked down on that lovely valley from the hillside, the whole scene around me charmed me.
The little wood opposite — how delightful to sit in its shade!
How fine the view from that point of rock!
And that lovely chain of hills, with the exquisite valleys at their feet!
If only I could wander and lose myself among them!
I went, and came back without finding what I wanted.
Distance, my friend, is like the future.
A dim vastness lies spread out before our souls.
The perceptions of our mind are as blurred as those of our eyes, and we long to surrender our whole being, to have it filled with the complete and perfect bliss of one glorious feeling.
But alas, when we have reached the thing, when the distant there has become the present here, everything is changed.
We are as poor and as hemmed in as ever, and our souls still thirst for a happiness they cannot reach.
75: So the restless traveller longs for his native soil.
And he finds in his own cottage, in his wife's arms, in his children's affection, and in the work needed to keep them, the happiness he had searched the whole wide world for in vain.
76: In the morning at sunrise I go out to Walheim and gather the peas in the garden with my own hands for my dinner.
I sit down to shell them, reading my Homer between handfuls.
Then I pick a saucepan out of the kitchen, fetch my own butter, put my mess on the fire, cover it up, and sit stirring it as it needs.
And I picture to myself the illustrious suitors of Penelope, killing and dressing and cooking their own oxen and swine.
Nothing fills me with a purer or more genuine sense of happiness than these touches of patriarchal life which — thank Heaven — I can imitate without affectation.
It is a happy thing for me that my heart can feel the same simple, innocent pleasure as the peasant whose table is covered with food he grew himself.
He does not merely enjoy his meal.
He remembers with delight the happy days and sunny mornings when he planted it, the soft evenings when he watered it, and the pleasure of watching it grow day by day.
78: The day before yesterday the physician came out from the town to visit the judge.
He found me on the floor playing with Charlotte's children.
Some of them were scrambling over me and others were romping with me, and as I caught and tickled them they made a great noise.
The doctor is a formal sort of person.
He arranges the pleats of his ruffles and keeps settling his frill while he talks to you.
He thought my behaviour beneath the dignity of a sensible man; I could see it in his face.
But I did not let myself be disturbed.
I let him go on with his wise conversation while I rebuilt the children's card houses for them as fast as they knocked them down.
Afterwards he went about the town complaining that the judge's children were spoiled enough before, but that now Werther was ruining them completely.
79: Yes, my dear Wilhelm, nothing on this earth touches my heart like children.
When I watch what they do, I see in these little creatures the seeds of every virtue and quality they will one day need so badly.
In the stubborn one I see the future firmness and constancy of a noble character.
In the capricious one I see the lightness and gaiety of temper that will carry him easily over the dangers and troubles of life.
Their whole nature is simple and unspoiled.
And then I call to mind the golden words of the Great Teacher of mankind: "Unless you become like one of these!"
And now, my friend, these children, who are our equals, whom we ought to take as our models — we treat them as though they were our subjects.
They are allowed no will of their own.
Where does our exclusive right come from?
Is it because we are older and more experienced?
Great God, from the height of your heaven you see great children and little children and no others; and your Son declared long ago which of them give you the most pleasure.
But they believe in him and do not listen to him — that too is an old story; and they bring up their children in their own image, and so on.
80: Goodbye, Wilhelm; I will not tangle myself any further in this subject.
82: The comfort Charlotte can bring to an invalid I feel in my own heart, which suffers more from her absence than many a poor creature lying on a sickbed.
She has gone to spend a few days in the town with a very worthy woman whom the doctors have given up, and who wants Charlotte near her at the end.
Last week I went with her to visit the Vicar of S—, a small village in the mountains about a league from here.
We arrived around four o'clock.
Charlotte had brought her little sister with her.
When we came into the vicarage courtyard we found the good old man sitting on a bench before the door, in the shade of two large walnut-trees.
At the sight of Charlotte he seemed to gain new life: he got up, forgot his stick, and ventured to walk toward her.
She ran to him and made him sit down again.
Then she took a place beside him, gave him a number of messages from her father, and caught up his youngest child — a dirty, ugly little thing, the joy of his old age — and kissed it.
I wish you could have seen her attention to that old man.

She raised her voice because he is deaf; she told him of healthy young people carried off when no one expected it; she praised the virtues of Carlsbad and approved his plan to spend next summer there.
And she assured him that he looked better and stronger than when she last saw him.
Meanwhile I paid my attentions to his good lady.

The old man was in high spirits; and since I could not help admiring the beauty of the walnut-trees that cast such a pleasant shade over our heads, he began — with some little difficulty — to tell us their history.
"As to the older one," he said, "we do not know who planted it; some say one clergyman, some another."
"But the younger one, there behind us, is exactly my wife's age: fifty years old next October."
"Her father planted it in the morning, and in the evening she came into the world."
"My wife's father was my predecessor here, and I cannot tell you how fond he was of that tree; it is quite as dear to me."
"My wife was sitting under that very tree, on a log of wood, knitting, when I came into this courtyard for the first time as a poor student — just twenty-seven years ago."
Charlotte asked after his daughter.
He said she had gone with Herr Schmidt to the meadows, and was out with the haymakers.
The old man took up his story again, and told us how his predecessor had taken a liking to him, and his daughter likewise, and how he had become first the man's curate and then his successor.
He had hardly finished when his daughter came back through the garden, together with the Herr Schmidt he had mentioned.
She welcomed Charlotte affectionately, and I confess I was much taken with the look of her.
She was a lively, good-humoured brunette, quite capable of amusing one for a short stay in the country.
Her lover — for that is plainly what Herr Schmidt was — was a polite, reserved person who would not join our conversation, for all Charlotte's efforts to draw him out.
What annoyed me was to see in his face that his silence came not from any want of ability, but from caprice and ill humour.
This became very plain later, when we set out for a walk and Frederica joined Charlotte, with whom I was talking.
The worthy gentleman's face, which is naturally rather sombre, went so dark and angry that Charlotte had to touch my arm and remind me I was talking too much to Frederica.
Nothing distresses me more than to see people torment one another.

Worst of all when they are in the flower of their age, in the very season of pleasure, and waste their few short days of sunshine in quarrels and disputes, and only see their mistake when it is too late to repair it.
The thought stayed with me; and in the evening, when we came back to the vicar's and sat round the table with our bread and milk, the talk turned to the joys and sorrows of the world.
I could not resist speaking bitterly against ill humour.
"We are apt to complain," I said, "though with very little cause, that our happy days are few and our evil days many."
"If our hearts were always ready to receive the good that Heaven sends us, we should gain the strength to bear the evil when it comes."
"But we cannot always command our tempers," said the vicar's wife. "So much depends on the constitution: when the body suffers, the mind is ill at ease."
"I grant that," I went on, "but we must treat such a disposition as a disease, and ask whether there is no remedy for it."
83: "I should be glad to hear of one," said Charlotte. "At least, I think a great deal depends on ourselves; I know it does with me."
"When something annoys me and upsets my temper, I hurry into the garden, hum a couple of country dances, and it is all right with me at once."
"That is just what I meant," I replied. "Ill humour is like laziness: it comes naturally to us."
"But once we have the courage to rouse ourselves, the work runs fresh from our hands, and we find real enjoyment in the very activity we shrank from."
Frederica listened very attentively, and the young man objected that we are not masters of ourselves, and still less of our feelings.
"What we are talking about is a disagreeable feeling," I added, "which everyone would gladly escape; but nobody knows his own power until he has tried it."
"A sick man is glad to consult his physician, and will submit to the strictest regimen and the most nauseous medicines in order to get his health back."
I noticed the good old man leaning forward, straining to hear our talk, so I raised my voice and spoke directly to him.
"We preach against a great many crimes," I said, "but I cannot remember ever hearing a sermon preached against ill humour."
"That may do very well for your town clergymen," he said. "Country people are never ill-humoured — though it might be useful now and then, to my wife for instance, and to the judge."
We all laughed, and he laughed very cordially himself, until he fell into a fit of coughing that interrupted our conversation for a time.
Herr Schmidt took the subject up again.
"You call ill humour a crime," he remarked, "but I think you use too strong a term."
"Not at all," I replied, "if the name belongs to anything so harmful to ourselves and to our neighbours."
"Is it not enough that we lack the power to make one another happy?"
"Must we rob each other of the pleasure we can all make for ourselves?"
"Show me the man who has the courage to hide his ill humour, who carries the whole burden of it himself without disturbing the peace of those around him."
"No: ill humour comes from an inward sense of our own want of merit, from a discontent that always goes with the envy that foolish vanity breeds."
"We see people happy whom we have not made so, and we cannot bear the sight."
Charlotte looked at me with a smile; she had seen the feeling with which I spoke, and a tear in Frederica's eyes urged me on.
"Woe to those," I said, "who use their power over a human heart to destroy the simple pleasures it would naturally enjoy!"
"All the favours and all the attentions in the world cannot make up for the loss of a happiness that a cruel tyranny has destroyed."
My heart was full as I spoke.
The memory of many things that had happened pressed on my mind and filled my eyes with tears.

"We ought to say to ourselves every day," I cried, "that we should not interfere with our friends, except to leave them in possession of their own joys and to increase their happiness by sharing it with them!"
"But when their souls are tormented by a violent passion, or their hearts torn with grief, is it in your power to give them the slightest consolation?"
84: "And then comes the last fatal illness, seizing the creature whose untimely grave you yourself prepared."
"She lies before you, weak and exhausted, her dim eyes raised to heaven, the damp of death on her pale forehead."
"And there you stand at her bedside like a condemned criminal, with the bitter knowledge that your whole fortune could not save her."
"And the agonising thought wrings you, that all your efforts are powerless to give the departing soul a moment's strength, or to quicken her with even a passing consolation."
85: At these words the memory of a scene like it, which I had once witnessed myself, fell on my heart with full force.
I buried my face in my handkerchief and hurried out of the room.
I was brought back to myself only by Charlotte's voice, reminding me that it was time to go home.
How tenderly she scolded me on the way for the too eager interest I take in everything!
She said it would do me harm, and that I ought to spare myself.
I will do so for your sake.
